questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) State and explain Four(4) factors affecting the supply of plantains in a local market in Cameroon.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Supply is the quantity of plantains that farmers and traders are willing and able to offer for sale at each price in a given period. It is affected by the following factors (2 marks each: 1 for stating and 1 for explaining).

1. **Weather and climate.** Plantains depend on rainfall and sunshine. Good rains give high yields and increase supply; drought, floods or storms destroy plants and reduce supply.

2. **Cost of production.** The prices of inputs (labour, suckers, fertiliser, pesticides, tools) and the cost of transport to the market. A rise in costs reduces profit and so reduces supply (the supply curve shifts left), and a fall in costs increases it.

3. **State of technology and farming methods.** Improved varieties, fertilisers, disease control and better storage increase yields and supply; traditional methods keep output low.

4. **Prices of other crops (competitive supply).** Farmers can use the same land to grow cocoyams, cassava, maize or cocoa. If the price of one of these rises, some farmers switch from plantains and the supply of plantains falls.

5. **Pests, diseases and natural disasters.** Diseases of the plant and pests destroy the crop and reduce supply.

6. **Government policy.** Subsidies on inputs and good extension services increase supply; taxes on farmers and bad rural roads reduce it.

7. **Number of producers and transport and storage conditions.** More farmers increase supply; bad roads and poor storage cause plantains, which are perishable, to rot before they reach the market and reduce the quantity supplied.

(Any four, each stated and explained.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) (i) State and explain Three (3) factors affecting the Elasticity of supply of a commodity.

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Elasticity of supply** measures the responsiveness of the quantity supplied to a change in price: $PES = \dfrac{\%\text{ change in quantity supplied}}{\%\text{ change in price}}$. It depends on the following factors.

1. **Time period.** In the short run, producers cannot change output quickly, so supply is inelastic; in the long run they can build factories, plant new crops and hire workers, so supply is more elastic.

2. **Availability of spare capacity and stocks.** If firms have idle machines or stocks of unsold goods, they can increase output quickly when price rises and supply is elastic; if they are already producing at full capacity, supply is inelastic.

3. **Ease of switching factors of production (mobility of factors).** If land, labour and capital can easily be moved from one use to another, supply is elastic; if they are specialised, supply is inelastic.

4. **Nature of the product.** Manufactured goods can be produced more quickly and so have a more elastic supply than agricultural goods, which depend on a growing period (cocoa takes years to bear fruit) and the weather. Perishable goods cannot be stored and have inelastic supply.

5. **Ease of entry of new firms.** If new firms can enter the industry easily, supply responds more to price increases.

(Any three, each stated and explained.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(ii) State and explain Three (3) uses of price elasticity of demand to the producer.

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Price elasticity of demand (PED)** measures how much the quantity demanded changes when the price changes: $PED = \dfrac{\%\text{ change in quantity demanded}}{\%\text{ change in price}}$. It is useful to the producer in the following ways.

1. **Pricing decisions and total revenue.** If demand for the product is **elastic** (PED greater than 1), a fall in price raises total revenue, so the producer should lower the price; if demand is **inelastic** (PED less than 1), a rise in price increases total revenue. For example, a supplier of salt or kerosene, for which demand is inelastic, can raise prices without losing much of the sales.

2. **Estimating the effect of a tax or of a cost increase.** If demand is inelastic, the producer can pass on most of the tax or of the higher costs to consumers by raising the price; if demand is elastic, the producer must absorb part of it, because a price rise would cause a large fall in sales.

3. **Price discrimination.** A producer can charge a higher price in the market where demand is inelastic and a lower price in the market where demand is elastic (for example, different prices for students and for other adults, or for peak and off-peak periods) and so increase total revenue.

4. **Forecasting sales and planning output.** Knowing the PED, the producer can estimate how much sales will change after a price change, and plan production, stocks and labour accordingly.

5. **Advertising strategy.** Producers try to make demand less elastic (by brand loyalty and advertising) so that they can raise prices more safely.

(Any three, each stated and explained.)
